terminal.description: A terminal in your workspace. `node try.js WATER_PRICE=2.10 water-bill.js 2400` runs `water-bill.js` with the setting `WATER_PRICE` in its environment, the same way in every terminal, and shows both streams and the exit code.

tasks.title: Read the price from the environment
tasks.description:
The water company charges by the 1000 litres, and its price changes every April. Write `water-bill.js` so that it reads the price from the setting `WATER_PRICE` in its environment and prints what the litres typed after the script's name cost, with two figures after the point. With `WATER_PRICE` set to `2.10`, `node water-bill.js 2400` prints:

```
2400 litres cost 5.04.
```

When `WATER_PRICE` is not set, the script prints one line on standard error that names `WATER_PRICE`, nothing on standard output, and ends with exit code 1.

Try it with `node try.js WATER_PRICE=2.10 water-bill.js 2400`. Check runs `water-bill.js` with prices and litres of its own, and once with no `WATER_PRICE` at all.
nextSteps: Read `WATER_PRICE` from `process.env`, and the litres from `process.argv`.
Find out what the setting holds when it is not set, and refuse that case first.
Turn both into numbers and work out the cost of the litres.
Print the line with two figures after the point.
hints: A setting the script was not given is `undefined` in `process.env`, like a missing argument in `process.argv`.
`process.env.WATER_PRICE` is text, like an argument. The price is for 1000 litres, so the cost is the litres divided by 1000, times the price.
`if (process.env.WATER_PRICE === undefined) { console.error('WATER_PRICE is not set.'); process.exitCode = 1 }`, and in the else, `(litres / 1000 * price).toFixed(2)`.

tasks.title: Refuse a price that is not a number
tasks.description:
A setting is text, and people type it wrong. Change `water-bill.js` so that a `WATER_PRICE` that is not a number above 0 is refused, the same way as a missing one: one line on standard error that names `WATER_PRICE`, nothing on standard output, and exit code 1. That includes a word like `two`, a price written with a comma like `1,80`, a price below 0, and a setting that is there but empty, which counts as not set. A good price still gives the bill.

Check runs `water-bill.js` with prices like those, and with one good price of its own.
nextSteps: Try `node try.js WATER_PRICE=two water-bill.js 2000` and look at what it prints now.
Turn the setting into a number, then decide whether that number is a price.
Find out what `Number('')` and `Number('1,80')` give, and make sure both are refused.
Refuse the price before anything is worked out or printed.
hints: `Number('two')` is `NaN`, and so is `Number('1,80')`. But `Number('')` is `0`, and `parseFloat('1,80')` is `1`.
`Number.isFinite(value)` is false for `NaN`. A price is also more than 0, and an empty setting is treated like a missing one.
`const price = Number(text)`, then `if (text.trim() === '' || !Number.isFinite(price) || price <= 0) { console.error(...); process.exitCode = 1 }`.

tasks.title: Warn about a leak, with a default limit
tasks.description:
A bill for a lot of water usually means a dripping tap. Change `water-bill.js` so that when the litres are more than the setting `LEAK_LITRES`, it prints the bill as before and also one line of warning on standard error, such as:

```
More than 5000 litres: check the taps for a leak.
```

It still ends with exit code 0. When `LEAK_LITRES` is not set, or is empty, the limit is 5000. When it is set to something that is not a number above 0, the script refuses it the way it refuses a bad price, naming `LEAK_LITRES`.

Check runs `water-bill.js` with `LEAK_LITRES` not set, empty, set to a limit of its own and set to a word, with litres below, at and above each limit.
nextSteps: Read `LEAK_LITRES` from the environment, and use 5000 when it is not set or empty.
Turn it into a number and refuse it when it is not one above 0.
After the bill, compare the litres with the limit, as numbers.
Print the warning on standard error, and leave the exit code alone.
hints: `??` gives the value on its right only for `undefined` or `null`, so an empty setting gets through it as `''`, which `Number` turns into 0.
Treat `undefined` and empty text the same, then use 5000. The check you wrote for the price can check this setting too, if it takes the setting's name.
`const text = process.env.LEAK_LITRES; const limit = text === undefined || text.trim() === '' ? 5000 : Number(text)`, then `if (Number(litres) > limit) console.error(...)`.

tasks.title: Show the settings, never the key
tasks.description:
The water company's account key is in the setting `WATER_KEY`. It must never show on the shed screen. Write `settings.js` so that `node settings.js` shows whoever sits at the laptop how the water scripts are set up, one line per setting, in this order:

```
WATER_PRICE: 2.10
LEAK_LITRES: 5000 (default)
WATER_KEY: set
```

`WATER_PRICE` shows its value as it is set, or `not set`. `LEAK_LITRES` shows its value, or `5000 (default)` when it is not set. `WATER_KEY` shows only `set` or `not set`: its value, or any part of it, is never printed, on either stream. The script ends with exit code 0.

Check runs `settings.js` with all three set to values of its own, and with none set, and looks for the key in everything it printed.
nextSteps: Print one line for `WATER_PRICE`, with its value or `not set`.
Print the line for `LEAK_LITRES`, saying when the default is in use.
For `WATER_KEY`, decide only whether it is there.
Run it with `node try.js WATER_KEY=abc123 settings.js` and make sure `abc123` is nowhere.
hints: `console.log(process.env)` prints every setting in the environment, secrets included. Print only the three you need.
A secret is not shown even in part: not its first or last letters. Whether it is set is all a person needs to know.
